articles.description: Andy Burnham needs a radical vision of economic change to move on from policies aimed at giving voters ‘breathing space’ Ask Andy Burnham a question and it won’t be long before he mentions the cost of living. Responding to the results of midterm elections in the US earlier this month, he said that the Democratic party’s triumph meant that there was “an opportunity now to unite around the issue that is affecting us all, and that’s the cost of living”. This wasn’t a non sequitur. The Republicans lost control of Congress in large part because Donald Trump failed to address concerns about the cost of basic goods – a failing aggravated by the US president’s disastrous war against Iran, which caused a spike in commodity prices, exacerbating the affordability problem. articles.title: The Guardian view on the next UN secretary general: sacrificing principles will damn the institution, not save it | Editorial
articles.description: The UK must continue to oppose the UAE’s tainted nominee, Lana Nusseibeh. The ethical course is also the pragmatic one The future of the United Nations has rarely looked more perilous in an age of impunity for atrocities, raging wars, open US hostility, a funding crisis and security council deadlock. It is widely agreed that the choice of its next secretary general is critical – perhaps even existential. Unfortunately, that’s where agreement ends. Under the opaque selection system, security council members are privately polled on their views of each candidate. A “discourage” vote from one of the five permanent members is diplomacy-speak for a veto. Only when a consensus emerges does the general assembly get a say on the candidate. The next straw poll is due on Monday, with no deal yet in sight . With António Guterres completing his term on 31 December, the seat could fall empty for the first time. Its soundtrack, however, is another story: a compilation of brand new material from some of the biggest pop, rap, rock and country artists on the planet – some of them combined in imaginative pileups of guest features – that can be enjoyed totally separately from the gameplay, if you so wish. articles.title: Anselm Kiefer review – Holocaust-haunted forests and a glimpse into a gigantic grave
articles.description: White Cube Bermondsey, London Kiefer asks what art means after the Holocaust – but even the vast scale of his powerfully seductive paintings can’t do justice to the gravity of his themes When the world is falling apart, the artist retreats to the studio. It’s an old story, and Anselm Kiefer has always loved the old stories, drawing for his monumental and reliably blockbuster paintings on narrative traditions ranging from Norse mythology to German Romantic poetry. So it makes sense that an artist who has dedicated his life to the question of what art means after the end of European civilisation – which is to say, after the Holocaust – should now seek out the solitude of the studio to make sense of what’s coming. Kiefer’s exhibition at the same gallery a decade ago had the title Walhalla , after the beer hall in the sky in which dead Vikings drink away the afterlife. Now comes the more modest (you would think) subject of the artist’s studio, depicted here in a suite of lustrous landscapes and a simple wooden cabin in the forest. Rendered in flat gold leaf, the sky in these paintings gleams like a tarnished halo in an old altarpiece, while the verdigris grass pushes roughly off the canvas. Here is the place where heaven meets the earth and is transmuted – by the alchemy of this painter’s touch – into quietly numinous paintings containing elements of both. If you can put aside the fact that Kiefer’s own studio is a vast warehouse complex on the outskirts of Paris, these paintings present a very German vision of communion with nature. They also evoke the most famous hut in modern philosophy: the Black Forest hideaway where Martin Heidegger formulated his argument that “authentic” culture must be rooted in the native landscape. articles.title: Influencers Behaving Badly at No 10? Burnham could have worse problems | Emma Brockes
articles.description: For all the fuss, it makes perfect sense for the PM to engage young people through TikTokers. He’ll have the last laugh on this one These are dangerous times to be a prime minister. So it is perhaps reassuring that the trouble into which Andy Burnham barrelled this week is so old school as to be almost soothing. Four months into his premiership, Burnham has arrived early at that rite of passage: the catastrophic attempt to engage with popular culture and subsequent category-5 storm in a teacup. After footage emerged of Influencers Behaving Badly at Downing Street, Burnham, in my view, has come out of the whole thing in surprisingly good shape. To recap: earlier this month, Burnham held a reception for social media influencers, one of whom, Luke Hamnett , was permitted to film himself doing the Hugh Grant dance from Love Actually before sitting down to interview the prime minister. Meanwhile, self-described “presenter, podcaster, idiot” Max Balegde filmed himself outside the door of No 10 miming what, in the words of the Daily Mail as it geared up to go the full Judge Pickles, “appeared to be a viral meme song”. These words were “bomboclaat pussywagon chicken nuggets”, which, as the Telegraph took a breath from its own meltdown to explain, turns on “a Jamaican profanity popularised online”. articles.title: They belong to Jerusalem’s past and present: meet the African Palestinians
articles.description: Despite militarisation, occupation and marginalisation, African culture prevails in the Old City, something I discovered first-hand when I visited Don’t get The Long Wave delivered to your inbox? Sign up here In occupied East Jerusalem, I met an often overlooked community: African Palestinians. This week, I explore their unique history, and how they are, in a classic diaspora fashion, integrated and marginalised in equal measure. There are about 450 African Palestinian people in occupied East Jerusalem, mostly living in the historical buildings of the Old City, near al-Aqsa mosque. That mosque, the third holiest site in Islam after those in Mecca and Medina, is the reason they are there. While Christians make up a small part of the African Palestinian population, most African Palestinians descended from Muslim pilgrims who came to East Jerusalem in the early 20th century (before Israeli occupation), and stayed either to tend to the mosque, or to continue Islamic practice and devotion within the city’s religious ecosystem. articles.title: Bill Bailey is an absolute master of musical mischief – this crowd hangs on every twang
articles.description: SEC Armadillo, Glasgow The comedian’s new concoction, Vaudevillean, mixes offbeat historical diversions, topical gags and virtuoso musical flights with warmth and absurdity Is any act ever really too niche for stardom? What could be more leftfield, after all, than Bill Bailey’s animated pop-musicology, with demonstrations on the Swedish nyckelharpa and the one-stringed Indian lute? But tonight he has yet another arena crowd hanging on his every strum, drumbeat and twang. Nothing need be niche, perhaps, if communicated with the open-hearted curiosity and passion Bailey brings to his esoteric interests. Add a flair for improbable juxtaposition, and a sense of humour that dusts curmudgeonliness with surrealism, and you’ve got a concoction that thousands-strong audiences find difficult to resist. The 61-year-old’s current show is called Vaudevillean, and gestures are made towards justifying that title, with reference to the French poet Olivier Basselin and the 1453 battle of Castillon. (You don’t get this with Michael McIntyre.) Like vaudeville, the show certainly has variety to recommend it. But really, this offering differs little from many a previous Bailey outing , and finds our host again following his nose from one unlikely musical experiment to another, via nuggets of topical standup and anecdotes from his storied life. Touring Europe until 2 May Continue reading...

articles.title: The unexpected joy hiding in Grand Theft Auto VI’s chaos? A little routine
articles.description: Rockstar’s latest blockbuster makes the everyday business of shopping, working out and taking care of a pet snake as compelling as its shootouts and car chases I knew I’d need many skills during the opening hours of Grand Theft Auto VI, but effective time management was not one of them. From playing the previous five titles in the series (and their many spin-offs), I understood I’d have to master Rockstar’s idiosyncratic approach to car handling. True enough, the vehicles do drive like airbeds tied on top of supermarket trolleys. I also knew I’d need to get to grips with the somewhat tricky aiming and shooting if I was to commit any sort of respectable crime spree. But for the first few hours of playing this staggeringly large and bewildering game, what concerned me most was lead character Jason’s personal routine. Each day, he needs to get up, choose an outfit, complete a workout, feed his pet snake Dolores, and perhaps do some DIY, so that when his girlfriend Lucia gets out of jail she’ll fall for him again – rather than fall through his apartment’s rotten staircase. Meanwhile, his drug-smuggling boss phones every five minutes with new parcels for Jason to pick up or drop off, and his pals Cal and Donnie get into all sorts of cocaine-related hijinks they expect Jason to extricate them from. There are also predatory neighbours to do favours for, and groceries to buy. I’ve seen so many people on social media posting about how they took several days off work to play this game, only to find themselves busier and more productive than ever. On his radio show last week, James O’Brien derided himself for completing, in Jason’s apartment, a simple DIY task that he’s put off for months in his own home. I know where he’s coming from. articles.title: The 4thWrite short story prize winner – a tale of teenage girlhood
articles.description: Read Darkroom by Meher Iqbal – this year’s winner of the Guardian and publisher 4th Estate’s award for unpublished writers of colour Meher Iqbal wins 2026 4thWrite prize with ‘evocative’ coming-of-age story • Content warning: This story includes a description of a sexual assault Nadia and I lay on the asphalt road, playing our favourite game for the last time. My older brother Abdullah had taught it to me when I was nine: lie down on a speed bump, legs long and both arms outstretched by your ears, making your body a long pencil. I was in the wrong position that day – it was so hot that the backs of my shins seared when they touched the road, so I had to bend my knees. Nadia wasn’t allowed to have her legs exposed anymore, so her linen trousers protected her. The game was intuitive – when you hear a car coming, roll down the slope and run away as fast you can. If you turned around only to find that the car was a decent way away, you were a baby. Abdullah never explained the underlying objective to me, but I think he enjoyed how much it agitated and scared adults at the same time. Simple and stupid, like most things he taught me at that age, but I liked that it gave me an opportunity to see just how fast I could run; the 100-metre track at school never drew out of me what running for my life did. Nadia didn’t care about any of that, but she humoured me anyway. Continue reading...

articles.title: 14th review – Ava DuVernay takes on a bully president and his viper’s-nest court of Maga sycophants
articles.description: DuVernay’s follow-up to her dissection of the 13th Amendment to the US constitution is a vehement and exhilarating defence of democracy Ava DuVernay’s previous documentary 13th , energised by the Black Lives Matter movement, was a brilliant polemic about the 13th Amendment to the US constitution , which she argued perpetuated a link between slavery and prison for African American men. Ten years later, and after an almost continuous decade of Trumpism, DuVernay has made a follow-up film about the 14th Amendment , and she has evidently arrived at a rather different attitude to the constitution and its authors’ intentions and good faith. Now she sees the enemy as Maga and the constitution as something that must be defended against a tinpot bully president and his viper’s-nest court of sycophants. The shift in view is not acknowledged, but the overall effect is similar. Utilising a gallery of very smart talking-head interviewees, including conservative Republicans, DuVernay has mounted a vehement and exhilarating defence of what might be called the second American Enlightenment, created by the 13th, 14th and 15th “reconstruction” amendments, drawn up between 1865 and 1870 after the American civil war. The 14th specifically established birthright citizenship, due process and equal rights for all races under the law, and furthermore barred insurrectionists from holding public office, all of which Trump appears casually intent on vandalising, airily amnesiac about his oath to uphold the constitution. Continue reading...

Britons get many of the facts about migration wrong and Reform UK voters are the group who get these facts most wrong, according to new research published today by King’s College University and YouGov. Among Reform UK supporters, 57% think net migration rose significantly in the year to June 2025, compared with 11% of Labour supporters and 8% of Greens. Eight in 10 Reform supporters think that asylum seekers are prioritised for social housing, compared with 21% of Green supporters. It is wrong to believe that if we could only correct misperceptions, we would automatically reduce concerns about immigration or policy preferences – because that misdiagnoses a large part of the cause, that these divides are partly driven by deep differences in values and identity. articles.description: Reinstated CEO tells staff ‘I made some terrible mistakes’, as questions remain over chips-to-China accusations. Chuck Schumer has accused Jensen Huang , the newly reinstated Nvidia CEO, of shipping “extremely advanced chips to China” and violating US export control laws. On Tuesday, the senator said the move “amounts to the equivalent of selling rocket engines to the Soviets during the space race”, adding: “This is an unfathomable failure of enforcement by the Trump administration.” What did Huang say to Nvidia staff on his return? He apologised and acknowledged he violated the company’s code of conduct by having extramarital affairs, but pushed back on reports that Donald Trump was instrumental in his reinstatement as chief executive. “I made some terrible mistakes,” he said. “I was unfaithful to Lori, and I hurt my kids and, of course, I hurt all of you.” How has the market reacted now? Technology shares led a market retreat on Tuesday as caution returned after Huang’s extraordinary return to Nvidia days after he was forced to resign, with investors bracing for further volatility in a key sector driving economic growth worldwide. The Great White Hope, which ran on Broadway from 1968 to 1970, was based on the life of Black boxer Jack Johnson, who in 1908 became world heavyweight champion in segregated America. Alexander played Eleanor, a white woman married to an African American boxer also called Jack, at a time when interracial marriages were still illegal in many states. articles.description: Another day and, despite all the promises, another damning report on the Met. There will be a reset: the public won’t be brushed off any more and neither will I In March 2023, Baroness Louise Casey published her damning review into the Metropolitan police. The review – which I commissioned after a series of appalling scandals – called for systemic reform to a failing organisation unable to tackle the profound problems it faced. But yesterday’s independent follow-up report by Dr Gillian Fairfield shows that, while the Met has made some important improvements, nowhere near enough has been done. I agree. Fairfield’s report concludes that the Met remains institutionally racist, sexist and homophobic. This will be acutely concerning for communities across the capital. articles.title: ‘I had to reject a lot of shame’: Michaela Yearwood-Dan on queerness, Catholicism and her extravagant artist dinner parties
articles.description: The artist adorns her luscious paintings with diaristic notes and confessions. Ahead of an exuberant new show she discusses their unique creation method – and the hunt for her missing cat The artist Michaela Yearwood-Dan is on the hunt for her missing cat. Pinto disappeared from her home in east London a couple of weeks ago and has so far defied the forecasts of tarot readings and the “witchy ladies” predicting his return. A lost pet is not the only thing she’s searching for. “I’m at a stage of life where I’m looking for answers” she says on the eve of her exhibition The Practice of Liberation, at Towner Eastbourne. Her other, more existential questions are those of many women in their early 30s: “Do I want to have children? How do I want to have children? What does my future look like?” She is “big into astrology”, but recently her thoughts have turned to her Catholic upbringing in south London, which serves as a large theme of her exhibition, which debuted at the Whitworth Gallery in Manchester earlier this year. Religious ritual has always appealed to her, and her show uses paintings, ceramics and a musical composition by her friend and longstanding collaborator Alex Gruz to evoke the ritual space of a church. articles.title: Toddlers are not just little people. Their culture deserves respect | Arwa Mahdawi
articles.description: Small children do not appreciate it when you join in with their singing or throw away their pee-covered leaves. And only a brute would suggest one of them might be tired Nobody can be good at everything, can they? Take me, for example. While I excel at remembering useless facts, going down online rabbit holes and getting toothpaste on my shirt, my singing is so bad it makes small children cry. This is not hyperbole: my five-year-old has wailed on many occasions throughout her short life because I’ve had the temerity to sing along to various TV show jingles or songs. As it turns out, however, it may not just be the fact that I can’t hold a tune that’s upsetting her. I’m not saying that everything I know about parenting I learned from viral posts on the internet, but there was an illuminating tweet doing the rounds last week that said: “Today I learned if you try to sing along with a toddler when you have not been invited to do so, it is a sign of great disrespect in their culture.” I immediately went down an online rabbit hole and discovered various other people have made similar jokes . It’s a common issue. Continue reading...

articles.title: AI's shock-and-awe raid on maths looks like pride before a fall | Rafael Behr
articles.description: Machines are bulldozing through hard problems to assert the power of their tech bro creators, not to advance human knowledge In most walks of life, trying something 12,363,153,437,138 times and getting the same result is reason enough to assume it works every time. Not in maths, where a conjecture that holds up more than 12tn times looks very probably true but doesn’t qualify as proven. That was the status of the Riemann hypothesis, one of the most famous mathematical conundrums in existence, until last week . Then Levent Alpöge, a mathematician working at Anthropic, said he and his collaborator, Claude AI, had crossed the line from conjecture to proof. articles.title: ‘I needed to purge it out of me’: the shocking true story behind harrowing drama Josephine
articles.description: Writer-director Beth de Araújo witnessed a brutal sexual assault as a child and has turned her experience into one of the year’s most powerful movies The film-maker Beth de Araújo likens the personal experience that inspired Josephine, her disquieting second feature, to a slow-acting poison. Early one Saturday morning when she was eight years old, Araújo and her father were playing soccer in Golden Gate Park, near their home in San Francisco, when they heard a woman scream. Her father, a former Olympic runner for Brazil, told her to stay and bolted to help; Araújo, scared and alone, ran after him, and instead found the woman in a clearing, naked from the waist down. Araújo was too young to understand what had happened, but she knew something was wrong. So, too, does an eight-year-old Josephine, played by the remarkable newcomer Mason Reeves, in the one scene crafted exactly to Araújo’s memory: Josephine, confused and restless, observes as the woman tucks her hands under her legs to keep them from shaking. She is further confused when her father, Damien, played by the aspirationally everyman actor Channing Tatum, seems extra keen to return to their soccer game afterwards, one of many echoes of Araújo’s memory in this taut drama. In real life, Araújo’s father “put on a face, put on energy and made it seem fun,” she recalled. “And I was like: ‘This is so weird. Why is my dad being so extra fun right now?’” Continue reading...

articles.title: The Slightest Touch review – running marathons in Colin Farrell and Emma Fogarty’s odd-couple friendship
articles.description: The pair, who met in 2010, are shown preparing for the Dublin race to raise awareness of Fogarty’s epidermolysis bullosa in Rachel Fleit’s considerate documentary The personal scenes in this film from Rachel Fleit have been carefully controlled and curated, the privacy of both parties being important, for different and understandable reasons. But it is an unexpectedly intimate, emotional piece of work, a big-hearted odd-couple story, which is perhaps slightly more complex than at first appears. Emma Fogarty is a smart, garrulous woman from Abbeyleix in County Laois in the Republic of Ireland who has EB: epidermolysis bullosa, a rare condition which means that her skin is permanently, agonisingly painful and requires a daily calvary of bandaging and re-bandaging. While getting an award at the People of the year event in 2010 for her campaigning work educating the public about this illness, Emma met and struck up a friendship with Colin Farrell, a supporter and patron of the EB charity Debra Ireland . articles.title: Sali Hughes on beauty: lactonic scents will have you smelling like cream soda – in a good way
articles.description: These fragrances are on trend right now, and smelling creamy can, it turns out, be surprisingly pleasant When the fragrance world picks a theme, it goes in hard. In the space of one month, I had close to a dozen new “lactonic” (that is, milky or creamy themed) perfumes to try. Instinctively, I wasn’t keen – I haven’t touched a glass of milk since nursery school – and so I eased myself in with DedCool’s Mocha Magic (£24 for 15ml), which adds a shot of coffee to the brand’s Xtra Milk fragrance that I love. This is immediately creamy, rich and bittersweet, like tiramisu, right down to that same dry hit of cocoa powder at the back of the throat. As in life, the coffee wears off, but the vanilla, spice and woody notes hang around for an impressively long spell. As with almost everything right now, it’s sweet, but not overbearingly so. Phlur, so beloved by gen Z, has leapt onboard the trend with Heavy Cream (from £26), available in fragrance and scented body spray. This is creamy, obviously, but also very sweet and immediately brings to mind Swizzels Drumstick lollies and the retro fizzy drink American cream soda. If this sounds like a kids’ party from hell, blame me, because it’s actually perfectly pleasant, got me heaps of compliments and got better and mellower as the hours passed. If you’re a milk with three sugars sort of a person, I think you may love it. Continue reading...

articles.description: The Norwegian Nobel laureate’s sequel to Vaim explores what happens when a man is stripped of everything that tells him who he is Very strange things happen in Jon Fosse’s 2025 novel Vaim . A man meets a woman he secretly loved in his youth while running an errand in a nearby town. She asks him to take her away with him, to the place where they both grew up, on the boat he named after her. She wants to live with him, she tells him, even though she is married, and he has never admitted his feelings. This same man, in another section, has now died. The woman returns to her husband, and tells him he must get back with her, but he has to answer to the name she gave him when they lived together. He must also move into the home of the man she had left him for. “All was strange,” the husband admits, and decides those words should be on his tombstone. Indeed, all is – and remains – very strange to the reader: the powerlessness of these men before this woman they hardly seem to know; the randomness of the events in their lives; their spooky, dream-like surreality. But most of all: Fosse’s narrative choices that thwart easy rationalisation. Vaim Hotel is the second volume in the Nobel laureate’s loosely connected trilogy-in-progress set in the fictional Norwegian town of Vaim. articles.description: In this adaptation of the sci-fi franchise Michelle Yeoh and Hunter Schafer are on a quest to track down a group of replicants gone rogue. It’s a neon-filled world of beautiful doomsday visions Memory: the mother of the muses, and the heart of the Blade Runner franchise. Science fiction is forever asking what it means to be human and, in the future dystopia first painted by Ridley Scott’s 1982 movie, the answer is that we are what we remember: we are the experiences we preserve as a collection of short films inside our heads. In the original Blade Runner, Rachael (Sean Young) is devastated to learn that her childhood memories aren’t real, and she is therefore a robot “replicant”; in Denis Villeneuve’s sequel, Blade Runner 2049, K (Ryan Gosling) knows he’s a replicant but hopes his memories are a sign that he is something close to human. Blade Runner has always been relevant to the age of AI, in that its starting point is that enslaved robots have rebelled. But the new version, the story’s first expansion into television, is acutely topical in an era where we’re increasingly anxious about whether what we’re seeing – or reading – is the work of machines. Fifty years on from the events of the last movie, the replicants have won: “Blade runners” are now replicants hunting down disobedient humans rather than the other way around, and the capture and storage of human memories is illegal. As humanity dies, what it remembers has become valuable contraband. Continue reading...

His book combines a history of surfing with a memoir of love and grief; it is an account of his girlfriend Kristen Tuason, who died from bone cancer at just 24. There is something desperately sad in the film’s nostalgic mood: Dungo still in his 20s, already looking in the rearview at his youth like it’s a different universe. AJ (voiced by Will Sharpe) is a gawky teenager skateboarder who meets fun, outgoing Kirsten (Stephanie Hsu); she’s a surfer and helps AJ to overcome his fear of the ocean. Pretty soon, they’re a couple, hanging out with friends, surfing with a mixtape of sunny bright pop tunes soundtracking their teenage years. Then Kirsten is diagnosed with cancer and undergoes surgery to partially amputate her leg. When the doctors tell her she’s in remission, life goes on. Kirsten trains to be a nurse, while her brother opens a surf shop; another friend starts a craft beer business; AJ is working hard at art school. Life is ahead of them. Arguably, the film, directed by Phuong Mai Nguyen, is light on detail: characters’ facial expressions are illustrated in simple lines, the finer details of their personalities unsketched. By contrast, the ocean is rendered in spectacular depth and detail, in all its moods. There is a reverence for the sea and surfing here, and a gentle tapping into surfing’s spiritual side; a handful of gorgeous scenes in a palette of mushroom brown and grey tell snippets of its origins in Polynesia. You’re doing the planet a favour if you eat mackerel , sorry, cod, I mean haddock, no coley, make that pollack – oh, whoops! These choices might make you feel better about yourself. articles.title: Secrets by Bob Woodward review – the world’s most famous reporter reveals all
articles.description: The journalist who helped bring down Nixon on false starts, Watergate, and the art of cultivating a source ‘I have always disliked the term ‘investigative reporter’.” So writes Bob Woodward, one of the most celebrated reporters of our time – the man whose Watergate reporting with Carl Bernstein undoubtedly changed the US presidency and journalism itself for ever. His longtime boss, the Washington Post editor Ben Bradlee, disliked the term too: “All reporting is investigative,” Bradlee would say. The term conjures a certain sophistication, perhaps, but part of the beauty of a reporter’s work is how deceptively unsophisticated it can be. Secrets is a far-ranging, revealing memoir of an extraordinary career, but more than that, it is an ode to grinding it out – knocking on doors, asking and asking again, listening, taking notes, making notes on the notes, patiently following every lead to exhaustion. In a media ecosystem saturated with fast and flimsy takes, this feels like a tonic. The real star of his story, Woodward seems to insist, is the shoe leather. Continue reading...

articles.title: Post your questions for Danny Boyle
articles.description: The Trainspotting, Slumdog Millionaire and 28 Days Later director is preparing to launch his biopic of Rupert Murdoch’s early years as a British tabloid mogul. In anticipation of its New Year release, the director will be taking your questions You name it, Danny Boyle has probably directed a movie about it. He’s done zombies in 28 Days Later, astronauts hurtling towards the sun in Sunshine, a man trapped under a boulder in 127 Hours, a world without the Beatles in Yesterday and junkies in Trainspotting. Boyle was born in Radcliffe near Manchester in 1956, and was heading towards the priesthood until, aged 14, a priest of all people talked him out of it. Instead he went into theatre, became deputy director of the Royal Court, then swerved into television, directing Inspector Morse among other things. His first film, Shallow Grave, arrived in 1994; two years later Trainspotting tore British cinema a new one. In 2009, Slumdog Millionaire won him the best director Oscar. He also masterminded the London 2012 Olympics opening ceremony, somehow squeezing industrial chimneys, NHS beds, James Bond, Mr Bean and the history of British pop into one stadium. articles.title: ‘I was physically beating myself up before a take’: Rory Culkin on anxiety, fatherhood and his famous brothers
articles.description: The star of Lords of Chaos, Scream 4 and Gabriel was always drawn to the dark side. Is that why he seems happier in Hollywood than his better-known brothers – and why he loved making Nocturne with Stephen Graham? Rory Culkin is enjoying the autumn afternoon in a Manhattan park. The trees are a dazzling blur of yellows, greens, oranges and reds; the background silence is so pure you can hear it. “I’m here with my baby daughter, Havoc,” he says. “Havoc Moon.” I tell him that is the spookiest name ever. “Thank you,” he says. Culkin chuckles like a revving moped, his huge blue eyes lighting up. “Yes, it’s a weird one. I think she’ll probably be the opposite. A sweet, quiet girl. She’ll play a harp or something.” He explains its origin. “I just threw out names to my partner one night when we went to dinner. She wasn’t taking to anything. I then suggested Havoc, and she really liked it. She came up with the Moon part. When we got home there was fresh graffiti on the wall across the street saying ‘Havoc’, and I was like: ‘That is a sign from the gods – we’ve got to do it.’” Continue reading...

articles.title: ‘Working with Kanye West? Talk about intractable egos!’ Caroline Shaw: the Pulitzer-winning composer everyone wants to work with
articles.description: She has collaborated with classical giants such as Anne Sofie von Otter – and pop stars including Phoebe Bridgers. But what happened when Caroline Shaw hit ‘peak hamster wheel’? ‘Look at those!” gasps Caroline Shaw, standing next to me at an old steelworks in Germany’s industrial heartlands. Behind us are defunct concrete cooling towers and, in front, main buildings that sprawl off in a mix of brick and corrugated iron. But Shaw is looking upwards, awed by massive exhaust pipes looming overhead. This place, in the city of Bochum in western Germany, oozes post-industrial chic. These days it’s the Jahrhunderthalle , an arts venue where Shaw is performing later with the Attacca Quartet. For now the complex is shut, so we chat on a concrete bench. Intercepting Shaw, the youngest ever winner of the Pulitzer prize for music, is no mean feat: “in demand” is an understatement for this Portland-based US composer, singer, producer, violinist and viola player. Thirteen years since winning the coveted Pulitzer for Partita for 8 Voices – an exhilarating unaccompanied vocal work that mixes speech and singing, baroque dances and analogue versions of studio-mixed effects – Shaw has a CV like no other. articles.title: What do Brexit and an Australian cricket scandal have in common? Sometimes it’s right to reopen old wounds | Jonathan Liew
articles.description: Just like the ball-tampering scandal of 2018, the Brexit debate is back. The lesson here is that anything with a dodgy whiff about it will only come back Just move on. You lost, get on with it. Why rake up the past? And why, for the love of all that is holy, is Theresa May back on my television? Of all the many regrettable political figures to have surfaced over recent days, perhaps May has been most triggering of all: a bleak reminder of unhappier times. But of course she has been far from the only former prime minister lured from obscurity by the irresistible siren call of Brexit Revisited. David Cameron has been portending a “very long and painful argument”. “Divisive” and “all-consuming”, argued Rishi Sunak. Boris Johnson warned Andy Burnham – with no apparent sense of irony – that reopening the Brexit negotiations would be “wasting his premiership”. Here they come, the cast of the Tory remake of Avengers: Doomsday, presaging of rancour and paralysis from the people who brought us years of rancour and paralysis. Jonathan Liew is a sportswriter and Opinion columnist for the Guardian The Guardian’s year in review 2026 On Tuesday 1 December 2026, join Guardian writers Zoe Williams, Lucy Mangan, Jonathan Liew, Heather Stewart, Pippa Crerar and John Crace for an evening of candid conversations, witty remarks and surprises as we look back on the year’s defining stories. articles.title: Shame is the only punishment in Australian cricket’s sandpaper scandal | Geoff Lemon
articles.description: The time for formal measures has passed but all involved have betrayed the trust of a country whose Test team is sacred Cry havoc. But Cameron Bancroft did not let anything slip, not after close to a decade of keeping his mouth firmly shut. It was a deliberate, considered and lengthy deed of revelation that the former Test opening bat chose to publish in the West Australian newspaper on Wednesday, claiming to finally fill in a wealth of detail around Australian cricket’s 2018 cheating scandal that so many others seem to have gone to such lengths to keep concealed. It was also a devastating repudiation of Pat Cummins, a teammate of equivalent juniority to Bancroft during their few months playing together, but now the Test captain, who had delivered his own manifesto in spoken form at a press conference last week. That version of events, in which Cummins was adamant that he had never been aware of any kind of ball-tampering in Australian colours, was what pushed Bancroft from silence to speech. “It made me feel angry, betrayed and alone,” Bancroft wrote. “What I saw, experienced and lived with not only him, but everyone else on that tour in South Africa is not the public account he gave in his press conference and in the years previously.” Continue reading...

articles.title: The Guardian view on the Trump, Xi and Putin meeting: it may be a first, but it’s not progress | Editorial
articles.description: A trilateral gathering is good news for China and Russia, but bad for the US – and its traditional allies “Historic” is a neutral descriptor, not a favourable one. Things can be unprecedented for good reason. Donald Trump’s meeting with Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin in Shenzhen, China on Thursday will be the first time that the leaders of the US, China and Russia have gathered for talks as a trio. The trilateral on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit is striking, but it is not an achievement. The lack of a clear agenda is telling: the spectacle really is the substance. Mr Trump sees international affairs in terms of spheres of influence. This meeting reinforces the obvious conclusion for the rest of the world – that they don’t get to sit at the table, only to be on the plate. Mr Xi promotes the notion of a multipolar world. Others would be more sympathetic if all three governments were not determinedly undermining multilateralism. Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? articles.title: The Guardian view on ‘two-tier policing’: tackle the myth, don’t pander to it | Editorial
articles.description: Confidence in the system is being corroded by cynical campaigns and far-right propaganda – that is the challenge to be confronted There are many areas of policy where public opinion diverges from evidence. Voters overestimate rates of crime, for example. Many will be sceptical of politicians who say today’s streets are safer than they used to be, although that is the reality. The challenge is to find methods of persuasion that don’t belittle the experiences of people who are afraid, and don’t like to be told their fears are unfounded. But there is a different challenge that arises when the cause of public concern is a problem that doesn’t really exist. Many people are angry about “ two-tier policing ” in Britain, supposedly characterised by disproportionately severe enforcement against white people and leniency towards minorities. There is no evidence to support a systemic bias of that kind. By contrast, the data suggests an imbalance of fair treatment goes the other way. People of colour are underrepresented in the police, disproportionately targeted with stop-and-search policies and, if arrested, likelier to have force used against them. articles.description: Oscar-nominated director delivers a thoroughly unserious biopic, wasting Christian Bale and Sienna Miller’s talents John Madden was a beloved American original, the burly football coach who segued easily from Super Bowl burnout to television darling to the last name in gaming as the NFL was overtaking baseball as the national pastime. When he wasn’t crashing into family rooms on football Sundays and Thanksgivings to break down the game’s rough complexities into fun-sized morsels, he was pressing flesh with everyday Americans while barnstorming the country in his Madden cruiser – the coach bus he depended on to compensate for his well-documented fear of flying. That the Madden video game franchise outlived the avuncular Minnesotan , whose death at age 85 in 2021 was mourned throughout the sport, is as much a testament to his singular knack for teaching the game’s fundaments as it is to his willingness to bring his classroom to students, wherever they might huddle. articles.title: BMI was never meant to evaluate an individual’s health | Letter
articles.description: Clinicians should start with the patient in front of them to identify obesity, not rely on a 200-year-old method that was aimed at entire populations, says James Capon Your report on a better way to diagnose obesity is welcome, though it is worth remembering how we came to rely on body mass index (BMI) in the first place ( BMI alternative for identifying obesity ‘could prevent misdiagnosis in millions’, 11 November ). The index was devised in the 1830s by the Belgian statistician Adolphe Quetelet, who wanted to describe the “average man” across whole populations. He never intended it as a verdict on any individual’s health, and it was largely forgotten until 1972, when the American physiologist Ancel Keys, most famous for developing the diet-heart hypothesis, revived it and gave it its current name. Again, it was for population studies. Continue reading...

Jenkins dismisses the work of HMIs as merely a “sniff” of the air and a stroll back to Whitehall, showing a lack of knowledge about their role. HMIs are former school leaders, with a deep knowledge and dedication to educating children and young people. They are as far from the typical civil servant (if there is such a thing) that it is possible to get, and in any case are not based in Whitehall. Jenkins does at least suggest an alternative approach, unlike some who are calling for the abolition of Ofsted, but I really question whether he has thought it through. This version by director Ebenezer Bamgboye brings modernity with its sleek storytelling, but also nods to the ancient Greek drama O’Neill was emulating in his 1924 play about illicit desire and the father-son fight for land. articles.title: Instant gratification is ruining our lives – and for me it started with my CD player’s shuffle button | Adrian Chiles
articles.description: Not even a compelling TV drama can stop me from staring at my phone. But this urge started 40 years ago, with what was at first presented as a useful feature I blame the shuffle button. That’s what started me on the long road to a thoroughly scattered mind – generally unable to focus on anything for more than a few minutes or even seconds. I was always a bit like this, hence an ADHD diagnosis in later life. But back in the day I still managed to read a lot of books, watch long films and listen to whole records at one sitting. Now? Not so much. Actually, hardly ever. Even something on television that I’m really engaged in – a drama or a football match – can hold me for only a few minutes before I find myself scrolling on my phone looking for I know not what. articles.description: The 49th edition of the new music festival begins this weekend. Where else can you indulge in a world of pure imagination, see the future – and chat over a curry with some of contemporary music’s biggest names? The Huddersfield contemporary music festival – or hcmf , with contemporary-cool lower-case, as it’s styled – celebrates its 49th edition this month, turning the darkness of late November into a beacon of blazing new-music ambition in West Yorkshire. It’s a festival with an extraordinary history. Nowhere else in the UK could you have bumped into Karlheinz Stockhausen and his entourage in a pub in the late 1980s; nowhere else could you have sat in the audience alongside Björk at the town hall; in no other town might you have stumbled on Pierre Boulez, John Cage, Olivier Messiaen and Yvonne Loriod chatting about the best place to have a curry that night. articles.title: Twenty years ago, the Wii and PS3 predicted the future of gaming – did they get it right?
articles.description: Both launched in 2006, with contrasting visions of gaming – one focused on accessibility, the other on technical ambition – each leaving a lasting legacy • Don’t get Pushing Buttons delivered to your inbox? Sign up here The main focus of the games industry this week is, of course, the release of Grand Theft Auto VI – a game that could define the next decade for the industry. For this week’s newsletter though, I wanted to direct your attention two decades into the past. In November 2006, two console manufacturers launched their competing – and wildly different – visions of what the future of video games would look like. Twenty years later, it’s clear that somehow they were both right. And yet, in some ways, they were both wrong. For Nintendo, the Wii was the natural extension of its famous maxim, Kareta Gijutsu no Suihei Shikō – roughly translated as lateral thinking with withered technology. Coined by the company’s legendary engineer Gunpei Yokoi, father of the Game Boy, the phrase described a philosophy in which old tech could be combined with smart ideas to provide amazing new gaming possibilities. The Game Boy itself used a slow, old Sharp LR35902 processor and a sickly green monochrome screen, but it also came with Tetris and worked for ages on four AA batteries. With sales of 65m, it was vastly more successful than hi-tech rivals such as the Atari Lynx and Sega Game Gear. Continue reading...

articles.title: ‘Everything he said sounded like a song title!’ The rackety, romantic life of Bobby Charles, alligator-befriending bard of the bayou
articles.description: He was nearly an early rock’n’roll star but took a different path, from Fats Domino to the Band and pro-environment songwriting. As a career-spanning box set is released, those who knew him remember an American original ‘I was listening to Bob Dylan’s Theme Time radio show,” says Korey Richey, multi-instrumentalist with LCD Soundsystem, “and he said, ‘Bobby Charles is best known as a songwriter, but he has one of the most melodious voices ever transmuted into a piece of vinyl.’ I thought about it, and I agree: Bobby Charles was something else.” Something else, indeed. Charles (1938–2010) was unable to play an instrument yet wrote songs sung by everyone from Fats Domino to Etta James to Kris Kristofferson. Signed to Chess Records in 1955 aged 17, he was on the verge of becoming a star at the dawn of rock’n’roll, but a preference for living reclusively – with a pet alligator – ensured he vanished from sight, and his music has long been unavailable. “He was a very strange guy, a loner,” says one of his Louisiana contemporaries, 88-year-old Johnnie Allan. “He knew what he had and wouldn’t compromise.” Now a box set, The Bobby Charles Story, containing almost every recording Charles released, aims to establish the Cajun magus as one of the greats. But I assumed it had long since gone the way of AIM and Skype, its manual turn-by-turn guidance made obsolete by big tech. Proof of life came in January 2025, when Donald Trump issued an executive order renaming the Gulf of Mexico the Gulf of America – a change Apple Maps and Google Maps promptly adopted, while MapQuest … did nothing. articles.description: Wallace Collection, London A sword, a wine cooler, a dazzling fresco … only a museum with such a copious store of treasures could put on a display this rich without having to borrow Mounting a “store-cupboard” exhibition – choosing items from existing collections to make a new, contained display – can be a cheap and easy way for a museum to make something out of its existing resources, without the faff of securing loans or collaborating across the industry. In the case of the Wallace Collection, however, the store cupboard is so embarrassingly rich and diverse that strong displays such as this on Cosimo I de’Medici can be drawn from only a handful of its objects. The 19th-century collection of Sir Richard Wallace holds a notable number of medieval objects, but their display can seem – at least to contemporary eyes – like a cacophony of applied arts, armour and paintings, not to mention a ton of gilt. This Medici display is part of a new enterprise drawing out histories from the noise for singular focus, sensibly repurposing what was once the cloakroom (a previously wasted bit of prime real estate) as a new dedicated space. articles.title: Grand Theft Auto VI review – gaming’s most depraved world is now also its greatest love story
articles.description: With realism that defies belief, this vast game easily accommodates its trademark foulmouthed, OTT chaos – as well as new empathy for the fugitive couple at its centre Tell us: are you playing Grand Theft Auto VI? In GTA VI, Rockstar has created the most extraordinarily, indulgently detailed virtual world that we have yet seen. Reviewing it feels a bit like trying to review, say, Paris: it contains so many potential experiences that it’s hard to know where to start. If you had been spying on me playing this game over the past few weeks you may well have caught me robbing banks, shooting up a weed farm or tearing along the highway at sunset blaring Bad Bunny on the in-game radio, but you might equally have caught me doing squats at the gym, shopping, assembling a coffee table or walking along the beach eating ice-cream. There is such a multiplicity of things on offer here that it is difficult to nail down what this game definitively is. Is it an interactive crime movie? A city simulator? A driving game? A sort of absurdly expansive version of The Sims in which the people you’re dressing up and looking after just happen to be professional criminals? It will be different for everyone – that is the beauty of it. For me, though, this game is about Jason and Lucia, the fugitive couple through whom you experience all that Leonida has to offer. Jason is muscular, handsome, ex-military, steady and unflappable, sincere but spare with words. Lucia has been boosting cars since the age of 14, has a wicked sense of humour and takes zero bullshit. (Lucia is the scarier one; I found myself turning much more quickly to violence when playing as her.) articles.title: Van Eyck: The Portraits review – a jewel box of phenomenal death-defeating paintings
articles.description: National Gallery, London Bringing together all the pioneering master’s portraits for the first time reveals the way he clinically preserved monsters, merchants – even his wife – like flies in amber Tricks! Traps! Riddles! Jan van Eyck’s portraits look vividly real – but are full of secret messages. What do they mean? The stubble is tiny yet silver-sharp on the chin of an unknown old man whom Jan van Eyck painted in oils 600 years ago: so long after both are dead you can still see this bloke needs a shave. The hairs on top of his head are just as miraculously caught, varying individually in paleness and lankness. You feast your eyes on the sagging skin of his throat with its overhangs and shady gulleys like a rock formation. He is a wonder, a freak of nature and yet a perfectly ordinary person. So are we all banal and marvellous, mundane and impossible, suggests Van Eyck. The National Gallery has created a jewel box of a show bringing together all Van Eyck’s portraits as we define them – a painting of a person for its own sake. Yet portraitist was a long way from being his only job. Van Eyck painted stupendous religious works, including the Ghent Altarpiece that he collaborated on with his brother Hubert. These too have portraits in them, of real people in uncanny proximity to supernatural beings. You could argue this show cheats by cutting out that medieval context of prayer and faith. It’s also a great way for the gallery to show off that it owns three of his greatest portraits. Yet the result makes you see the utterly strange way he collects his slightly miniaturised people like flies in amber. Continue reading...

articles.title: Ta-Nehisi Coates on the shocking case that shattered his childhood and inspired new HBO documentary
articles.description: A 36-year fight for justice is explored in the galling HBO documentary When a Witness Recants. The three subjects and producer Coates explain how it unfolded For most of his life, the writer Ta-Nehisi Coates would occasionally think of a chilling episode from his childhood in West Baltimore: almost exactly 43 years ago, on 18 November 1983, a 14-year-old boy named DeWitt Duckett was shot and killed in a hallway of Harlem Park junior high school in the middle of the afternoon, by an older teenager who stole his blue satin Georgetown jacket. Coates was only eight at the time, too young to know the details, but old enough to perceive the collective horror around him. The sensational event – the first time a kid was killed inside a Baltimore public school, according to wall-to-wall local press – was a rupture in his child’s view of the world. “It was first time I had the sense that, oh, actually, I exist in a very dangerous world,” he told the Guardian. “And then you cut to the TV and it’s clear the rest of America is not existing in that dangerous world. The dangerous world is only for you and people who look like you.” Coates always assumed that the three teenage boys arrested and convicted for the murder were the right guys, and the episode faded into one of those strange imprints from the past, a blurry but foundational event. Continue reading...

Originally written in Greek and Arvanitic, a dialect spoken by a Greco-Albanian ethnic group, and featuring characters from an unspecified Arvanite village, it was a hit in Greece in 2014 and comes to the UK in an agile translation by Siân Valvis. In her fascinating introductory note, Valvis writes of her attempt to capture the “unruly, galloping force” of Dimosthenis Papamarkos’s prose. She succeeds in thrilling style. Delivered in a demotic, gossipy voice, these are rough-hewn stories of ambushes and vendettas, of brothers in arms being “closer than kin” and of lingering, sour regret. One of the translations of the eponymous Arvanitic word “ gjak ” is “blood” and indeed, graphic bloodiness is inescapable. Back in September, Turkish authorities began a large-scale crackdown on LGBTQ+ organizations and activists, raiding offices, blocking social media accounts and websites, arresting at least 116 people and launching criminal investigations into at least 160 people. Meanwhile, since last month, Turkey’s last two remaining opposition television channels have been brought under government control. This follows the Turkish government’s widespread crackdown on the main opposition party with dozens of mayors arrested since 2024. Despite Turkey’s authoritarianism, in Antalya, many of the Turkish groups critical of the government gathered in large numbers at the People’s Climate Summit, an alternative gathering to the U.N. climate summit organized by a coalition of Turkish environmental groups. articles.title: Childhood neglect, unmet needs, mental health struggles: this is the making of a Neet | Mark Mon-Williams
articles.description: As a researcher for the Milburn review, I’ve seen how we’ve failed a generation – then castigated them. Britain must break this vicious cycle Mark Mon-Williams is chair in cognitive psychology at the University of Leeds and professor of psychology at Bradford Institute of Health Research Alan Milburn and Peter Fonagy have, between them, expertly diagnosed the UK’s illness. Their reviews show we don’t just have a Neet crisis. Or a school absence crisis. Or a Send crisis. We have a neglected childhood crisis that will wreck the country’s long-term prosperity if we just keep patching over these symptoms. The solution to any problem starts with understanding its causes, and Milburn and Fonagy provide a thoughtful analysis. I have worked closely with both of them, being a topic group member for Fonagy’s independent review into mental health conditions, ADHD and autism, and supporting Milburn with data analytics. Their reviews have followed the evidence, all of which shows a system neglecting children at scale. We have decreased benefits and slashed the support provided to children: today 4.5 million children are living in poverty. When these children grow up and are diagnosed with anxiety and depression, impeding their ability to work, they are often castigated as feckless snowflakes. It is easier to do this than admit that we have failed a generation, and that this is the predictable consequence of political decisions. articles.description: Scientific discoveries are explained effortlessly in this portrait of a man whose research was driven by pure passion Niels Bohr shares with Albert Einstein pride of place in the pantheon of 20th-century science. The two had much in common. They were not expert mathematicians; they prized physical intuition over mere competence; and they did not shy away from the moral and political implications of their work. But Bohr differed from Einstein in one crucial respect: his extraordinary personality. In his gripping biography Philip Ball ensures we feel the intense pull of Bohr’s genius. Solving problems is the raison d’etre of any scientist, but Bohr went far beyond that: having inaugurated quantum mechanics with his model of the atom in 1913, he simply would not give up until the rest of it was understood. articles.title: A moment that changed me: the tomato pasta that became an obsession – and helped me lead a better life
articles.description: At a restaurant in Italy in 2022, every forkful of my meal made my eyes close and mouth water. For four years since, I have tried to recreate this dish. The pursuit has finally made me a proper vegetarian I’ve ostensibly been vegetarian for 13 years and, in that time, I’ve eaten a lot of meat. My mum used to leave out the last bit of lamb madras, with a wink, then loudly announce that she was going to bed. I have accidentally found myself in KFC at midnight, hood up, drunk, looking both ways and asking for a Bargain Bucket. My partner once came home early from a night out and caught me red-handed, in bed with McDonald’s Chicken Selects. Such incidents were infrequent moments of weakness and, after the fact, I was always racked with guilt. But for most of my vegetarian life, I had felt a certain emptiness; a gaping meat-shaped hole in my heart and stomach. Then I ate a bowl of pasta. It was 2022 and an Italian university friend, Mattia, invited me to Tuscany. I spent four days with his lovely family, in the rolling verdant hills, with fireflies and fallow deer keeping us company, drinking vernaccia and talking of books and art and poetry. But none of that matters, not even a bit. All that matters is a single plate of tomato pasta from Nuova Trattoria Albana , in Mazzolla, west of Siena. This pasta might have seemed, to the untrained palate, like any other pasta. But it changed everything for me. Continue reading...

articles.description: In a world carved into continental blocs by authoritarians, Britain has to make common cause with its neighbours In the chronicles of 21st-century diplomacy few statements have caused as much offence with as few words as Barack Obama’s 2014 description of Russia as a “regional power” . Vladimir Putin’s politics were defined then, as now, by vengeful resentment of his country’s relegation from superpower status after the cold war. His worldview is warped by a paranoid conviction that Nato never stopped striving to deepen that humiliation, even after the USSR had unravelled. From his Kremlin throne, the Russian president expects to be treated as a colossus of world history. It is hard to overstate how bitterly he hated being dismissed by Obama as a geopolitical B-lister. articles.description: Eyjafjörður: Our boat was surrounded by around 15 of them, exploding their exhalations out of the water – and numbers are increasing here For the first half-hour, Eyjafjörður, Iceland’s longest fjord, offered few signs of marine life – just three cormorants and a raft of common eiders. Then, suddenly, there it was. A distant spout of water vapour. A humpback whale . As we motored out, more bushy plumes appeared to port and starboard, until we found the boat surrounded by about 15 individuals. Cutting the engine, the captain announced that he was about to employ a secret technique to coax the whales closer. There were raised eyebrows as the opening notes of Céline Dion’s My Heart Will Go On crackled over the speakers. But, as if on cue, two explosive exhalations erupted alongside the boat, prompting whoops of delight. Continue reading...

articles.description: In her new film, the actor plays a lawyer taking on the French state over reproductive rights. She talks about being criticised for her support of Israel and pushed to the limit by Lars von Trier While she was making the film Women on Trial , about the real-life trial of a child prosecuted for having an abortion, someone sent Charlotte Gainsbourg a photograph of her mother at one of the pro-choice demonstrations that erupted in France at the time. It was “very moving”, says Gainsbourg to see her mother, the actor Jane Birkin, in 1972, “looking beautiful and in the middle of a demonstration”. At that time, in a court in Bobigny, a Paris suburb, the prominent lawyer Gisèle Halimi was defending 16-year-old Marie-Claire Chevalier, as well as her mother and two other women who helped her have an abortion, then illegal in France. The Bobigny trial was new to her, says Gainsbourg, who plays Halimi, a leading figure in French feminism and activism who died in 2020. “I had no idea. For me, abortion rights started with Simone Veil” – the French minister of health who saw through decriminalisation three years later – “so I had to catch up.” Continue reading...

articles.title: Jess Cartner-Morley on fashion: this season’s big idea? Wear a skirt. It’s that simple
articles.description: All you need to look on-trend this autumn is a skirt, but instead of going shopping, check what you already have in your wardrobe I go to a lot of fashion shows, and sometimes they are gorgeous and sometimes they are ugly. Sometimes they are electrifying and sometimes they are deathly dull. Sometimes they are completely baffling. My absolute favourite kind of show is the one that makes me want to run home and change my outfit. A show that makes me think: there it is! That’s exactly what I want to wear. When the look speaks to me, as if it had been on the tip of my tongue. God, I love that. Which is what happened at Prada this season . The idea was: skirts. That’s it, that’s the whole idea. The show was 63 different skirts – some with a sweater, some with a bra top, some with a jacket, but the point was the skirts. They were knee-length, give or take an inch up or down, and A-line, although sometimes a narrow almost-pencil and other times with a broader flare. There were skirts that wrapped like kilts, held together with strips of industrial-weight Velcro embroidered with tiny gems. articles.title: Touch of evil: the terrifying truth about sleep paralysis
articles.description: One in five people have experienced this frightening state – and the Harvard neuroscientist Baland Jalal has dedicated his career to studying it. Could it be a portal to a deeper understanding of the mind? The Harvard neuroscientist Baland Jalal is considering the unfathomable depths of the human brain. “It can contemplate itself, and vast galaxies, spirits, souls, poetry, Einstein. Yet you hold it in your hand and it seems so trivial.” Jalal’s passion – the subject that drove him to become a scientist – is sleep paralysis, a brain glitch that can fill its host with terror so palpable that it can cause lasting trauma. “What you get very close to in sleep paralysis,” he says, “is that subjective world of the mind. It’s very hard to put into words.” He should know – he’s spent 271 pages trying to do so. His new book, The Phantom Mind, argues that by exploring the borderlands of sleep, where sleep paralysis occurs, we can delve deeper into how all aspects of our minds work. He may wear a lab coat and examine brain regions and neurochemicals, but studying the mechanics, he says, doesn’t damp down the mysteries of consciousness. “For me, actually, I’ve become more spiritual and interested in the world of mystery and, I want to say supernatural, but dimensions that are intangible, by studying something like sleep paralysis.” Continue reading...

articles.title: "Birds of War": New Film Tells a Story of Love and Journalism from Syria to Lebanon
articles.description: We speak with Janay Boulos and Abd Alkader Habak, filmmakers and subjects of the new documentary Birds of War , which tells their epic love story through years of upheaval in the Middle East. Boulos, a London-based Lebanese journalist working for the BBC , and Habak, a Syrian activist and cameraman, first connected while covering the Syrian civil war and stayed in touch through years of war, revolution and exile, forming a relationship that is chronicled in the documentary by drawing on 13 years of their personal videos, voice notes and other correspondence. The film also examines the unequal relationship between international news organizations and local journalists whose work they rely on, the fraught political history between Syria and Lebanon, and how Boulos and Habak’s personal connection overcame those divisions. “Without our journalistic relationship, [we] would have never been together. I would have never opened my heart to somebody like him,” says Boulos. “We can be any race, any gender, any religion, any background, but at the same time we’re all humans.” Birds of War premiered at the 2026 Sundance Film Festival, where it won the World Cinema Documentary Special Jury Award for Journalistic Impact.

articles.title: Meet David Morales: Providence Voters Elect Democratic Socialist Mayor, Approve Israel Divestment
articles.description: Voters in Providence, Rhode Island, approved a ballot measure last week that could result in the city divesting from Israel. The successful grassroots campaign makes Providence the first U.S. city to pass a binding divestment measure through a popular vote. The measure instructs the city to divest from countries and companies implicated in “ethnic cleansing, apartheid, illegal military occupation, or genocide.” The language does not mention Israel by name. We speak with one of the key backers of the divestment measure, Mayor-elect David Morales, a 28-year-old democratic socialist who made history on election night as the youngest mayor ever elected in Providence. “What we saw was our neighbors coming out in the thousands to demonstrate that we are ready for change,” Morales says, promising to enact his affordability-focused platform. “It’s the responsibility of local government to take action. His most impactful relationship, however, would prove to be with a young Donald Trump, whom he mentored in business and politics during the 1970s and ’80s. articles.title: "The Earth Shook Last Night": Talarico Wins Senate, Hinojosa Becomes First Latina Governor in Texas
articles.description: Texas Democrats have shattered more than three decades of Republican dominance in the state, winning races for U.S. Senate, governor, lieutenant governor, attorney general and even railroad commissioner. They are also poised to possibly take control of the Texas House of Representatives for the first time since 2003. The Republican governor of Texas, Greg Abbott, lost his bid for a fourth term to Democratic state Representative Gina Hinojosa, who defeated him by nearly 700,000 votes. She will be Texas’s first Latina governor. And James Talarico will be the first Democrat to represent Texas in the U.S. Senate since 1993. “We’re celebrating these wonderful candidates who won office, and we’re also starting to think about what it means to hold power,” says Mike Siegel, a city council member from Austin, Texas, who founded Ground Game Texas, a statewide voter turnout organization. “We need to start thinking very quickly about how we will protect public education, how we will stop data centers and the encroachment of AI on our society, how we will protect public schools, how we stop collaboration with ICE .”

articles.title: Abdul El-Sayed Becomes First Muslim Senator as Democrats Rout GOP Across the U.S. in Rebuke to Trump
articles.description: In a stunning repudiation of President Trump, Democrats regained control of both chambers of Congress in Tuesday’s midterm elections, flipping seven Senate seats: Iowa, Kansas, Ohio, Maine, North Carolina and South Carolina. Meanwhile, progressive Democrat Dr. Abdul El-Sayed defeated former Republican Congressmember Mike Rogers for an open Senate seat in Michigan with over 52% of the vote. El-Sayed campaigned on a platform of Medicare for All, tackling economic inequality and getting big money out of politics — as well as ending military aid to Israel. He is the first Muslim elected to the U.S. Senate. For the second time in four days, Mikel Arteta’s side found themselves a goal up at half-time and apparently coasting toward victory, only for their opponents to rouse themselves and earn a deserved draw. After Newcastle on Saturday , this time it was an impressive Borussia Dortmund who became only the second side to take points off Arsenal in their past 15 group stage games in this competition. It could have been worse had an offside flag not ruled out Jobe ­Bellingham’s goal after Max Beier equalised a thunderbolt from Viktor Gyökeres. But the much-maligned Sweden striker was guilty of a glaring miss late on as Arsenal laid siege to Dortmund’s goal, racking up 30 shots by the final whistle. The German side had to hang on for a result that gave their travelling fans a night to remember, although Arteta admitted his players must be more clinical when Real Madrid and Jude Bellingham visit north London in a fortnight. articles.title: The Guardian view on disability benefits: Timms’s radical review is rooted in experience | Editorial
articles.description: Ministers have taken on board their MPs’ message about cuts. Now anxious claimants need reassurance Four million people with disabilities or long‑term health conditions in the UK claim personal independence payment (Pip). A review by Sir Stephen Timms, the social security minister, offers a blueprint for how to overhaul it . Its recommendations pose a difficult question for ministers: are they prepared to meet the needs that a more accurate assessment of the costs of disability might reveal? Sir Stephen worked as one of three co-chairs with a steering group of 12 people with a range of professional and lived experience. There is broad agreement that Pip needs to be reformed. The announcement on Tuesday that the government would accept the recommendation of a new fast track for claimants whose conditions are lifelong or unlikely to improve, and abolish unnecessary benefit reviews, signalled that ministers are ready for change. The decision, affecting one in 10 claimants in England and Wales, is welcome but long overdue. Ministers should work with the devolved administrations to ensure similar progress elsewhere in the UK. articles.title: The Guardian view on Andy Burnham and Wales: a devolution blindspot at No 10 | Editorial
articles.description: The PM has summarily dismissed Welsh demands for further powers similar to those enjoyed in Scotland. The approach seems at odds with his consensual style As he headed for Downing Street this summer, Andy Burnham said that he aimed to be “as collaborative and pragmatic as possible” in his dealings with the governments of Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland. His predecessor, Sir Keir Starmer, had notoriously warned ministers against being “overly deferential” in discussions with the devolved administrations. But Mr Burnham’s signature commitment to distributing more power and responsibility out of Westminster, and his consensual style, appeared to augur well for a positive reset in relations. In Wales, this early optimism has just been brutally quashed by an uncharacteristically peremptory letter from Mr Burnham to the first minister, Rhun ap Iorwerth. In it, the prime minister flatly rejected Welsh calls for the devolving of powers in relation to policing and justice, the crown estate and rail infrastructure. In the case of policing, Mr Burnham is in the curious position of denying to Mr ap Iorwerth the type of power that he enjoyed as the mayor of Greater Manchester. articles.description: The reintroduction of the birds in England and Wales spells disaster for fragile marine ecosystems, warns Tim Birkhead Your article on white-tailed sea eagle reintroduction ( Reintroduction of white-tailed eagles puts seabird colonies at risk of wipeout, say experts, 8 November ) highlighted the risk that white-tailed sea eagles are likely to pose to Britain’s seabirds. To argue, as Prof Ian Convery and Rebecca Wrigley did in their responses ( Letters, 15 November ), that the re-establishment of white-tailed sea eagles will somehow restore a lost paradise is fallacious. Where is the evidence that sea eagles will restore that balance? There is no evidence. Also, suggesting that because in the distant past sea eagles and seabirds coexisted, their reintroduction will pose no problems is naive. By failing to acknowledge that past marine ecosystems were much more robust, and seabird prey more abundant, than they are today, these two authors miss the point that it is precisely because our seabirds are currently short of food that they are so vulnerable to disturbance and predation from white-tailed sea eagles. articles.description: Reform leader is happy to return to his anti-EU happy place, where the truth can be whatever you want it to be This feels like Nigel Farage’s happy place. It’s hardly a secret that he prefers his own company. His fellow Reform MPs are a necessary inconvenience at best. Muppets at worst. He can barely hide his misogyny for Sarah Pochin, having written her off as a pisshead. Nor does he have a much higher opinion of Richard Tice, Zia Yusuf and the others. But even Nige has worked out that when it comes to having a Potemkin alternative cabinet, he can’t realistically do everything himself. Only when it comes to Brexit, it seems, is Farage at his best as a one-man band. This is his battle. During Monday’s Commons statement, Andy Burnham said he didn’t want to keep “banging on about Europe”. But Nige most definitely does. Not least because the more he can talk about Brexit, the less people will criticise him for having no real plans for government. Most of his domestic policies collapse on contact with reality. As for foreign policy, he doesn’t have one. Unless you count having as little to do with the EU as possible. The Guardian’s year in review 2026. articles.title: Mariella Frostrup calls AJ Odudu ‘aggressive’ – and here we go again. We tire of this angry black woman trope | Natalie Morris
articles.description: Microaggressions pile up, and then they are triggering. Amid the latest row on I’m a Celebrity, we’re obliged to explain this hurt all over again When I heard Mariella Frostrup call AJ Odudu “aggressive” over the weekend on I’m a Celebrity … Get Me Out of Here!, my heart sank with sick recognition. For her part, AJ’s mother has since said that watching her daughter experience this all-too-familiar dynamic was a “living hell”. I know many Black women tuning in will have felt a collective shudder of disgust and solidarity. Of course, there is pushback. “Our addiction to offence is tearing us apart,” wrote a Telegraph pundit on Monday . But, this language is not neutral. There is a long history of Black women having their conduct and tone disproportionately scrutinised by white people. And what happened between Odudu and Frostrup is a tale as old as time. A Black woman stands up for herself and, no matter how reasonably she presents her argument, she is accused of aggression. It is an efficient tactic to flip the focus on to the behaviour of the Black woman, and it is rooted in racist stereotypes. Natalie Morris is the author of Mixed/Other: Explorations of Multiraciality in Modern Britain Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? Why is his brilliance only now being recognised? Victorian industrial designer Christopher Dresser was always a visionary. As a child, he was so artistically gifted he went to design school in 1847 when he was just 13. articles.title: Why the genocide verdict against Myanmar has big implications for Israel | Geoffrey Robertson
articles.description: Proving the ‘crime of crimes’ against an individual is notoriously difficult, but the ICJ has set a precedent for states to be found liable. Israel could be next For the first time ever, a state has been found guilty of genocide – that “crime of crimes” – and has been ordered to compensate victims and to prosecute and punish the perpetrators. This judgment came from the international court of justice (ICJ), which has convicted Myanmar of killing and expelling many thousands of Rohingyas in Rakhine state in 2017 . The court did not change the definition of the crime, settled by the genocide convention in 1948 as requiring proof of an intention to destroy, in whole or part, a racial or religious group as such. But it made the prospect of proving this against a nation a good deal easier than against an individual. It set a precedent for its next case concerning state liability, namely the case brought by South Africa against Israel. Geoffrey Robertson KC was a UN appeal judge and is author of World of War Crimes – Eyeless in Gaza and Beyond Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? articles.title: What happened when the man who took a million photographs embraced colour?
articles.description: The Photographers’ Gallery, London Sanlé Sory is known for his black and white images taken during independence in Burkina Faso – but his colour portraits bring humour, insouciance and joy Despite his wide renown, there have been hardly any major exhibitions of Sanlé Sory’s work. His last UK show was in 2019, concentrating on the black-and-white images the Burkinabé photographer made in the first two decades after opening his own studio, Volta Photo, in Bobo-Dioulasso in 1960 – a period that coincided with the first two decades of independence in Burkina Faso. This new Photographer’s Gallery show shifts the focus to the 1980s and 1990s, when Sory began working in colour. It’s easy to see why, even with few exhibitions, Sory has made such an impression on audiences. There are the familiar west African studio photography tropes westerners love, where sound, image, fashion and pose collide. The props are popping, the style is irrepressible, the energy is irresistible. I wonder if Sory’s speed and instinct came from the time he spent early in his career racing on his motorbike to photograph car accidents for newspapers and the police. These portraits are the opposite of a car crash, they’re remedially joyful, wilfully alive – but they share that feeling of being inside the moment, at the edge of something. Continue reading...
