articles.title: The secret to the perfect Christmas party cocktail
articles.description: Festive drinks are all about capturing the warmth and theatre of the season, so lean into wintry flavours such as orange and cloves, and add a bit of drama by bringing out the blowtorch What are the best cocktails to make for a Christmas party? Dan, by email We’re all in favour of getting the party season started early, Dan, so now is as good a time as any to get your drinks cupboard in order. “Ultimately, Christmas cocktails are all about bringing a little warmth, nostalgia and theatre, so don’t be afraid to have fun with seasonal flavours,” says Josie Pink, author of River Cottage: Cocktails and Botanicals . The smell of orange, be it fresh or dried, is never too far away at this time of year, and one reason Pink suggests having a batch of orange liquor on hand, not least “to rustle up a margarita or two”. Ditto dried citrus wheels: “They’re a must,” she says. “Not only are they gorgeous for adorning cocktails, but any misshapes can be turned into marmalade dust, and any spares into home decorations.” Pink also advises getting some syrups in your arsenal – “I’d opt for a batch of trusty vanilla syrup” – plus a chai number “for those fragrant, warming spice flavours that we all associate with the festive season”. If there’s a gang coming over, you’ll likely find Pink ladling hot mulled apple juice laced with citrussy gin into mugs, or making pitchers of rum punch: “Either would warm the cockles.” Alternatively, consider a “slightly lighter” mulled white wine: “Gently warm your favourite white wine with spices such as star anise, cinnamon, ginger and cloves, sweeten with syrup and citrus, then spike with apple cider brandy.” Got a culinary dilemma? Email feast@theguardian.com Continue reading...

articles.title: ‘The lack of fun is as noticeable as the lack of content’: the reborn Museum of London is all piazza, no punch
articles.description: London Museum Smithfield Why has the revamped museum divided its exhibits into nonsensical themes and shunted all the fascinating stuff downstairs? The results are baffling, unengaging and soulless ‘ An astonishing sight’: Oliver Wainwright reviews the building’s architecture The Museum of London at the Barbican was the capital’s local museum, a crowded and quirky presentation of its history from the Dagenham idol to Vauxhall Pleasure Gardens . But apparently the location deterred casual visitors, and maybe it just wasn’t grand enough to reflect London’s self-conscious significance. For not since ancient Rome has a capital dominated its nation’s history and culture like London. So now we get the rebranded and reimagined London Museum Smithfield. History surrounds you in this neighbourhood: Black Death burials by the Charterhouse, the Knights of St John, the Smithfield martyrs, William Wallace’s execution site. So goodbye scruffy brutalist Slough House location, hello deep history. Except when you enter the new museum, all that history, all those layers going back to the Romans and earlier, have been brushed away. If you want an illustration that bigger is not better, this is it. When Sharon Ament, the director, asked me if I liked it, I couldn’t find the words. I was heartbroken, speechless, unlike the museum’s management who have their own way with language. Displays have nonsensical themes: “London as Ritual”, “London as Stage”, “London as Sunrise”. One wall text begins: “London is a city of people.” Read that twice. What is this? Cunk on London? Continue reading...

articles.title: Let’s hear it for the leftwing echo chamber | Zoe Williams
articles.description: By chance, I found myself committed to a debate with people whose views I share. It was an eye-opening experience I was on a panel recently in a church – St Luke’s in Battersea, south London – about the future of the welfare state, except the other panellists booked to speak on the right of politics were unwell and couldn’t come. And so we ended up with an entirely leftwing panel (albeit different shades of the left). Puckishly, I suggested that I would split my six minutes of allocated speaking time and do three on what the rightwing panellists would have said, had they appeared, and then three on why they are wrong. But I couldn’t get the arguments right. I know they think the current welfare bill is – between our ageing population, our Neets and our dated expectations about what a decent life looks like and whose job it is to ensure you have one – “unsustainable”. I just couldn’t summon the right mix of tough-minded realism and benign resignation to other people’s misery. It wouldn’t come out of my mouth. Continue reading...

articles.title: Crunch time: Niki Segnit’s five rules for winter salads
articles.description: Plus five fantastic recipes, from seared tuna and potato to spicy butternut and lentil, to show how it’s done Approach a winter salad as you would your winter wardrobe – with clever layering. With the greatest respect to Coco Chanel, and her famous rule about taking one item off when you think you’re done, in this instance I favour assembling a salad and then adding an ingredient. Unlike in baking, where departing from a recipe can have its risks, improvisation rewards the salad maker. Still, if you’re planning a winter salad, especially if it’s a main meal, you might want to use a checklist to avoid some common pitfalls. The most egregious of these is cosy dullness. It’s all too easy to throw together some fresh winter produce and end up with a dish that’s more like a cold risotto or yesterday’s traybake. This often comes down to the combination of roasted root vegetables and “interesting” grains. What makes a salad a salad is its invigorating qualities, but root veg and cereals are sweet, with earthy, nutty flavours and soft textures; the pairing might be a modern classic but it’s about as invigorating as a warm bath. Not that you should avoid the combination; you just want to balance it with ingredients that offset its soporific qualities. It’s a good stress test for our guidelines, in fact: if you can turn a root-and-grain combination into a bright and balanced salad, you’re on to a winner. Continue reading...

articles.title: ‘An extravagantly illuminated beast’: the best artificial Christmas trees in the UK – tested
articles.description: Pick wisely, and your fake fir could be reused for decades of Decembers. From pre-lit to frosted to space-saving, here are our festive favourites • The best beauty Advent calendars • The best Christmas baubles In the 70s and 80s Essex of my youth, no one had a real Christmas tree unless they lived in the country, or perhaps Loughton. Our family’s skinny artificial tree is now 55 years old and comes out every year at my sister’s. It’s shed a few plastic “needles” down the years, but it’s still standing proud – which is more than you can say for a real Christmas tree bought in 1971, or even 2025. Therein lies the surprising environmental efficiency of artificial Christmas trees. The Carbon Trust says using a fake tree over seven to 20 years (depending on its weight and materials) can create fewer emissions than buying a new, commercially grown tree every year. The key is to buy an artificial tree you’ll love enough to roll out for decades. Continue reading...

articles.title: To Hold a Mountain review – a spectacular setting for tough savvy woman’s fight against the government
articles.description: A livestock farmer with a sad secret in her past rallies to keep military training out of her breathtaking mountain home in Montenegro An award-winner in Sundance, where it premiered earlier this year, this slow-burn documentary follows a middle-aged Montenegrin livestock farmer called Gara and her 13-year-old daughter Nada. The two of them eke out a hardscrabble living on Sinjajevina, a breathtaking mountain plateau on which Montenegro’s government would like to conduct training exercises for its own army as well as Nato’s. This goes down about as well as a wolf in the sheep pen with flinty Gara, who rallies her neighbours as well as the local media to fight the proposal. She displays a savviness that’s somewhat surprising, even if her fortitude and strength of conviction seem completely in character. However, that fight against the state is just one element of a film that, through long, languid takes, reveals the women’s stately pastoral existence, one taken up above all with care for their menagerie of animals (cows, sheep, goats, cats and dogs) and each other. Co-directors Petar Glomazić and Biljana Tutorov gradually reveal the family setup isn’t exactly what it appears at first. Although Gara calls Nada her daughter, the young girl is actually her niece; Gara adopted her after her sister, Nada’s mum, was killed by a violent husband. Gara’s profound grief and loss haunt her every day, felt most painfully, perhaps, when an animal dies on the heath, reminding them of the fragility of life. Continue reading...

articles.title: Cookie fever! How does Marks & Spencer knock out so many viral food sensations?
articles.description: Chicken kievs, ‘picky bits’, strawberry and cream sandwiches: the hits have been coming for almost half a century. Now Kathryn Turner, M&S’s head of product development, has become a social media celebrity. What’s the secret ingredient? The scenes in a Liverpool Marks & Spencer , after the release of the chain’s chocolate and cornflake cookie earlier this month, looked like brink-of-Covid panic buying crossed with a zombie apocalypse. It probably didn’t help that the baked goods hit the shelves at around the time the government started asking Britons to plan for an unnamed near-term disaster . How would we cope with a national emergency when we coped this badly with the crisis of not enough biscuits? You could explain the M&S cookie fever with reference to the company’s product development icon, Kathryn Turner, who has half a million followers between Instagram and TikTok, or the powerful urge to belong, in gen Z particularly. But it surely has something to do with the biscuit itself. As Rosie Sykes, the author of The Friday Biscuit, says: “Biscuits are very much part of the national fabric.” But lately they’ve had this “slightly weird glow-up”, gone “a bit max”, Sykes says. Whatever the flavour, there is always chocolate in them, and always more of it than you’d credit. Even the packaging on the M&S cookies – clear, crinkly – has the main-event feel of a bouquet or a hamper. Except if you put these cookies in a box, that box would be ginormous, and people would say: “I can’t eat five of those – don’t be stupid.” Continue reading...

articles.title: The World of Love review – beautifully directed and compellingly elusive family mystery

It seems always to be gesturing at an indefinable sense of loss, a poignant keynote struck by the recurring soundtrack piano arrangement of Bach’s Sheep May Safely Graze. Seo Su-bin gives an excellent performance as Joo-in, a high schooler possessed of a cheeky, madcap sense of fun, like her wacky, magic-obsessed kid brother Hae-in (Lee Jae-hee). She is keen on taekwondo and often shown (in borderline-uncomfortable closeup) kissing boyfriends that she will later dump. But when classmate Su-ho (Kim Jeong-sik) asks her to sign a petition objecting to the release and local rehousing of a convicted child rapist, Joo-in refuses, on the ostensible grounds that the petition talks about the permanent damage done to rape victims. Joo-in astonishes and upsets the class by announcing at the top of her voice that she herself is a rape victim, and she has not been permanently damaged – and then says it was just a joke. But residents still believe it’s worth fighting for The kitchen in the Alman family farmhouse is large, airy and decorated with hundreds of rosettes awarded over the decades for prize-winning dogs, sheep and cows. I grew up just up the hill, so I know this kitchen well. Apart from the video feed in the corner, showing what the cattle are up to in the barn, it hasn’t changed much since the 1980s when we’d pile in here after helping our fathers with the baling. From the kitchen, Gladestry’s small, slate-roofed primary school, set against the steep green slope of Hergest Ridge, is clearly visible, and – it being playtime when I visited – clearly audible too. That hasn’t changed much either since the days when Joseph Alman and I were pupils at that tiny school, and our own parents looked out of that same window and heard us calling to each other as we played football. The US and the UK had been publicly warning their allies for weeks about what Russia was planning, as well as threatening the Russians with a wave of sanctions unprecedented against a major power. Putin’s foreign policy had long relied on confusion and untruth. By saying that they knew exactly what he was up to, Britain and America were hoping first to deny him his usual ambiguity, and second to pressure the men around him into making him stop, since war would deprive them of the stolen assets they’d stashed in London’s most exclusive neighbourhoods. The audio was recorded over the summer during a labor and hunger strike organized by immigrant detainees. Junior Marte, an asylum seeker and father from Venezuela, was one of the organizers. He describes conditions inside the facility, including abusive treatment, medical neglect and prolonged legal limbo. “We are here unjustly, wrongfully accused of being criminals. Yet immigration officials refuse to review our cases, because they know that we are all innocent people,” Marte says in the message. The hunger and labor strike lasted for a month, with an estimated 300 detained immigrants participating in the protest. Jenny Garcia, campaign coordinator at the American Friends Service Committee of New Jersey, says that since the strikes, GEO Group and ICE have taken “every opportunity to retaliate against the strikers, the families visiting outside, and the protesters.”

articles.title: Too Big to Fire? Jensen Huang Is Back at Nvidia; Questions Loom Over AI Boom & U.S.-China Relations
articles.description: Nvidia stock prices surged over 30% on Monday as the chip maker reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO . Huang had stepped down earlier in November amid reports he had multiple extramarital affairs, including with a woman accused of spying for China. Huang and Nvidia have been central to the AI boom, and the leadership turmoil had erased trillions in value from the U.S. stock market. President Donald Trump acknowledged he had encouraged the company’s board to bring Huang back. “The fact that our markets are so over-indexed on the AI trade, that something like three-fourths of gains in the [S&P 500] this past year have been AI-related, is unsustainable,” says Aya Ibrahim, senior fellow for economic and national security at the AI Now Institute. We also speak with organizer and researcher Tobita Chow, who says Huang’s “spy scandal” that led to his ouster is part of a larger effort by anti-China figures in the U.S. national security establishment to escalate tensions between the countries. “The national security leadership in both parties in D.C. has been greatly frustrated with President Trump, who has over the past year pursued policies to maintain very warm relations with Xi Jinping,” says Chow, who notes that Secretary of State Marco Rubio is one of the “chief” frustrated China hawks in the administration.

articles.title: Children of the revolution: how the north of England is defining modern men’s fashion
articles.description: Once the historic centre of the textile industry, the north is now home to a host of a provenance-driven labels. But is there a specific northern menswear look? And what does it all mean for the mad-fer-it stereotypes? In 2026, clothing has proved more important to Andy Burnham’s political identity than that of any British prime minister since Margaret Thatcher. He is a loyal Clarks and Adidas wearer, whose Howick worker’s jacket hangs in Manchester’s People’s History Museum. His ousting of Keir Starmer – launched shortly before being photographed jogging in a replica Everton shirt – has been memorialised as the “casual coup”. In one telling, the reason for this is simple: he’s a man from the north. That Burnham is the first born-and-bred northern male PM since Harold Wilson last swished his Gannex raincoat out of Downing Street goes some way to explaining his higher interest in clothing. It’s not necessarily that all men in the south care less about clothing, or that all men in the north do – but that many men from the north express it in such a distinctive, even unified, way. articles.description: These ancient and often grossly unfair taxes are stifling the economy and young people. It’s long past time for radical reform When voters were asked in 2020 which tax they would cut first , council tax came out on top, and rightly so. Still, it’s taken six years for an array of Labour and Liberal Democrat MPs to call for reforms to this most grotesquely unjust tax. Prompted by a public petition organised by the campaign Fairer Share, a Westminster Hall debate heard calls for a review into property taxes, which would lay out options for replacing council tax and stamp duty land tax. Labour MPs were among those who have signed a letter to Downing Street calling for property tax reform to be a priority in Andy Burnham’s upcoming 10-year plan . Among flotillas of economists and thinktanks who signed the letter is Lord O’Neill, a Burnham adviser and former Goldman Sachs economist, who calls UK property taxation “utterly nonsensical”. Burnham has frequently backed reform of the “highly regressive” council tax and stamp duty, labelling them as “a tax on the aspiration of young people”. articles.title: Why I love Rome in winter: ‘We reclaim the city and slip back into familiar routines’
articles.description: There is plenty of sunshine, the tourists have thinned out – and no one does a traditional Christmas like the Romans There was a time when, during a Rome winter, I would crave the warmer months. Not any more. The combination of intense heat and overtourism has made summer poco piacevole , as Italians would say – not very pleasant. So come mid-September, when the temperature drops and the crowds thin out, our mood lifts as we reclaim the city and slip back into familiar routines. In winter, the temperature is mostly mild and there is still plenty of sunshine (we do tend to grumble if the rain and grey skies persist for a few days). Rome is best seen on foot, and my favourite time to walk it is on a Sunday. Until earlier this year, I lived in Esquilino, a vibrant neighbourhood close to Termini train station. I’d begin with coffee at Gatsby Cafe by Piazza Vittorio before walking along Via Merulana – a tree-lined street similar to a Parisian boulevard – and then through the Colle Oppio park, past the Colosseum and towards Circo Massimo . articles.title: The pest I’ll never forget: the cockerel whose crowing almost destroyed me
articles.description: When a neighbour installed a braying bird on the roof of our block of flats, the noise was relentless from sunrise till sunset. It became the sinister soundtrack to my life You can’t choose your family or your colleagues. And you definitely can’t choose your neighbours: the people with whom you involuntarily share a postcode and the ritual of swapping misdelivered Amazon parcels. For the most part, the neighbours in my block of flats are reassuringly neighbourly. During lockdown, I became unofficial IT support for one trying to home-school her son. I spent years emailing a PR man about Guardian celebrity interviews without realising he lived two doors away. And one of my neighbours (and now my hero) used to be in the 80s punk band Splodgenessabounds, who sang Two Pints of Lager and a Packet of Crisps Please. The other half I couldn’t pick out of a police lineup, although I certainly know their habits, from the phantom non-recycler who bungs all their plastic bottles and newspapers in the normal black bin, to the mystery resident who happily leaves the security gate open. But the one that is lodged most firmly in my memory is the neighbour who, last year, kept a pet cockerel on the roof. At least, I assume it was a pet. I can’t think of any other reason that doesn’t sound considerably more sinister. Continue reading...

articles.title: The Song of Stork and Dromedary by Anjet Daanje review – don’t miss this glorious epic inspired by Emily Brontë
articles.description: The afterlife of a Yorkshire village girl who becomes a gothic literary icon is explored across three centuries, in a thrilling paean to the power of books I had a plan. I was going to nibble away at this great wedge of a book, a morsel a night, like a little reading mouse. But then the story swallowed me whole. I read Dutch author Anjet Daanje’s The Song of Stork and Dromedary over three feverish nights, and spent the days in between longing for the dark. This 720-page novel should come with a warning label: may cause severe infatuation. We begin in the fictional Yorkshire village of Bridge Fowling with Susan Knowles-Chester, a woman who attends to the dead. The year is 1847, and Susan knows the old ways, the threshold rituals: how to arrange a corpse so it doesn’t gape and gawp at the living. “The villagers have a horror of her work, for wherever she goes, she leaves grief like driftwood in her wake, yet when the time comes, many ask for her help, it is an open secret.” Continue reading...

articles.title: TV tonight: friends Prue Leith and Sandi Toksvig take a special holiday

I have been ill recently, and while my natural inclination is to cook food that I want to eat, our bodies are clever organisms and, as is often the case, the food we crave is often the food that our systems need. Unlike the federal budget, where we get plenty of notice of when it will be handed down, the government only gives us a few days notice for the mid-financial year economic and fiscal outlook (or Myefo). There’s still a fair bit of work to do to finalise it all, but we’ve made enough progress to be confident that at this stage there will be a modest net save in the budget. We’re not going to slash and burn in the budget where that would impact the payments that people receive or where it would impact some of the more sensitive parts of the economy. articles.title: Take me to the fatberg! The £437m new Museum of London is an astonishing sight
articles.description: After a 10-year transformation, the glorious cathedral-like Smithfields market is now telling the capital’s story. Our architecture critic enters a world of jewels, axes, DJs and dog races – with unposh coffee from Syd’s century-old stall ‘All the grit and the glitters,” trumpets a big illuminated sign on the roof of the old Smithfield general market, beaming out as if advertising a raunchy burlesque show. It is the jazzy tagline of the new-look London Museum, which has gone from being marooned on a roundabout in an armpit of the City to taking over this prime Victorian market complex, following an arduous decade-long transformation. The slogan is fitting for a museum that displays everything from priceless Tudor jewels to a lump of congealed fat and rags dredged from a Whitechapel sewer. Just as the colossal fatberg was scraped from the murky depths, so has the former market hall (and its extensive warren of basement vaults) been meticulously scoured and scrubbed up. London’s centre of butchery for 800 years, which Charles Dickens found “all asmear with filth and fat and blood and foam”, has been lavished with a £437m glow-up, reborn to tell the story of the capital in all its gritty, glittery glory. And the finished result is an astonishing sight. Continue reading...

articles.title: The Last Spy review – a riveting tale of CIA meddling, espionage gossip and Blue Nun wine
articles.description: Refugee Peter Sichel was known as ‘the Jewish James Bond’ after fleeing Germany and becoming an integral cold war-era spy. He died last year but, at 100-years-old, he told his remarkable story for this film Why, exactly, was Peter Sichel “the last spy”? It’s not something Katharina Otto-Bernstein’s documentary about the cold war-era CIA man clarifies. The “Jewish James Bond” – as a woman from his synagogue nicknames him – is a catchier moniker, although that’s not quite right either. If Sichel was once a swashbuckling secret agent, we don’t hear much about his escapades here. Instead, he seems closer to M: sitting behind a desk pulling strings while his agents risked life and limb sneaking around the German Democratic Republic. The Last Spy begins as a straightforward but riveting biography built around a long, candid interview with Sichel, who was 100 at the time of filming (he died last year at 102). We hear about his childhood in Germany, which was initially privileged thanks to his great-grandfather’s lucrative wine business. Yet his mother was spooked early on by the rise of Hitler, and insisted the family relocate to France. When war did break out, all Germans were considered “enemy aliens” and sent to internment camps. Later, when the German army advanced, the Jews were allowed to make a run for it, pursued by warplanes. After hiding out near the Pyrenees, Sichel and his family escaped to New York in 1941 – only to find themselves living beside a Nazi-supporting neighbourhood on the Upper East side.
